name: Plasma transfusions (Blueprint)

image.caption: Wounded Marine receives a blood plasma transfusion (NCP 01361), National Museum of Health and Medicine (3385176109)

lead: Plasma transfusions in the Blueprint context are the anti-ageing experiment in which entrepreneur Bryan Johnson received plasma from his teenage son in 2023. Proponents of the idea hope that blood-borne factors from young donors can make tissues and organs act younger, which would show in skin, energy and general appearance.
The idea comes from mouse studies of joining young and old animals. Johnson reported seeing no benefits and said he would not repeat the procedure.

paras: In Johnson's case, a series of one-litre plasma transfusions was given over six months under medical supervision, including a family exchange in which his father received plasma from him. The wider young-plasma idea is usually carried out in clinics.

The FDA has stated that transfusions like this are without proven benefit and may be harmful. Plasma transfusion carries general risks such as allergic reactions, infection transmission and volume problems.

angle.text: Proponents hope that young plasma shifts the body toward younger biology, which would show as a younger appearance. In the Blueprint case, Johnson reported no benefit.

lead: Plasma transfusions in the Blueprint protocol refers to Bryan Johnson's 2023 experiment, in which he received monthly one-litre plasma transfusions over six months as part of his anti-ageing project. One transfusion was tri-generational: his 17-year-old son donated plasma to him, and he donated to his own father.[1]

The aim of such infusions is to slow or reverse biological ageing, which people see as extending to skin quality, vitality and look. Johnson later said he saw no benefits and would not repeat the procedure; the FDA has said transfusions like his are without benefit and may be harmful.[1]
The idea draws on heterochronic parabiosis studies in mice, which reported that exposure to young blood reversed some age-related impairments in brain, liver, heart and muscle.[2]
infobox: FDA: no benefit, may be harmful[1]

paras: Blueprint is the anti-ageing project announced by Bryan Johnson on 13 October 2021, with the stated aim of lowering the biological age of his organs.[1] Plasma transfusion was one of its experiments in 2023.[1]

Parabiosis studies joined young and old mice. Villeda and colleagues reported in 2011 that young blood improved cognition and synaptic plasticity in aged mice, and other work reported reversal of some impairments in several organs.[2]
Johnson received monthly one-litre transfusions over six months; his teenage son donated to him and he donated to his father. He later reported no benefit.[1]

No studies found specifically testing young plasma for appearance. Related research includes trials of plasma transfusion in trauma, such as the PAMPer pre-hospital plasma trial,[3] which concern bleeding rather than ageing.
The FDA has stated that transfusions like Johnson's are without benefit and may be harmful.[1] Some experts quoted on the Blueprint project are sceptical of its claims overall.[1]

timeline.event: Mouse study reports young blood improves cognition in old mice.[2]
Johnson receives monthly plasma transfusions for six months.[1]
